qt: to the Commission Claudiu-Richard Târziu (ECR) Subject:

Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Member States such as Romania are particularly exposed to high energy and administrative costs and have more limited access to finance, digital skills and qualified personnel. These constraints can make it difficult for them to adopt advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence. 1.

How will the Commission ensure that its simplification agenda produces measurable benefits for SMEs in Member States with less developed economies and does not disproportionately favour larger companies?
Will the Commission consider strengthening the ‘SME first’ principle by systematically assessing the administrative and financial impact of new EU legislation on SMEs?

What concrete financial, training and technical support does the Commission plan to provide to SMEs in countries such as Romania to accelerate the adoption of artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.11.2026) Simplification is a key priority for the Commission. The target is to cut recurring administrative costs, lowering the burden by at least 25% for all businesses and 35% for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Since the start of the mandate, 12 omnibus packages and other parallel simplification initiatives have brought proposed administrative costs savings to EUR 22.3 billion per year. The Commission has been using several tools to systematically assess the potential impact of new legislative proposals on SMEs and to identify mitigating measures where disproportionate impacts arise1. Amongst others, the Commission is developing good practices and model legal clauses for SME-friendly provisions, giving EU and national lawmakers concrete examples to use that correspond to the types of potential disproportionate impact flagged by the SME test2. The Digital Europe Programme3 funds digital infrastructure and skills in cohesion countries. Furthermore, around EUR 10 billion4 in the 2021-2027 cohesion policy programmes support productive investments in SMEs related to digital technologies, and digital skills and advisory support services. European Digital Innovation Hubs, including seven in Romania, help SMEs identify AI use cases, test solutions before investing, acquire relevant skills and access technical expertise. The Enterprise Europe Network5 provides SMEs free advisory, capacitybuilding and technology transfer services and support in accessing EU funding and alternative sources of finance. These complement support already given through Romania’s Recovery and Resilience Plan6, which includes measures to support digitalisation7, the microelectronics sector8 and research and innovation9. 1 The SME filter is applied when the Commission publishes its intention to legislate on the ‘Have Your Say’

portal and identifies which initiatives are relevant for SMEs and thus require a proportionate SME test. The SME test assesses the impact of new legislation on SMEs where an impact assessment is required. The SME check, a compulsory annex to impact assessment reports, summarises the key SME test findings for initiatives that are (highly) relevant for SMEs. In addition, targeted SME consultations, including panels supported by the Enterprise Europe Network, gather direct input on SME challenges. 2 Such as reporting burden, compliance cost, or access barriers for smaller companies. 3 https://commission.europa.eu/funding-and-tenders/find-funding/eu-funding-programmes/digital-europeprogramme_en. 4 Out of which EUR 7 billion from the EU budget. 5 https://een.ec.europa.eu/. 6 https://mfe.gov.ro/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/3d768db15a25839d401ffd1f095fd39f.pdf. 7 This support included grants of up to EUR 100 000 per SME to encourage the adoption of digital technologies, including advanced digital technologies. According to evidence submitted by the Romanian authorities, 4 561 SMEs received grants for digitalisation and 52 companies received grants for advanced technologies (https://reforms-investments.ec.europa.eu/document/download/a6a84573-7b33-4cbb-949f757ad7941569_en?filename=C_2026_3432_1_EN_annexe_acte_autonome_nlw_part1_v1_Redacted5.pdf). 8 Under the Important Project of Common European Interest on Microelectronics and Communication Technologies (IPCEI ME/CT), Romanian SMEs had the opportunity to take part in projects developed in cooperation with large companies and academia, contributing to the development of the country’s microelectronics ecosystem. 9 The established Centres of Competence promote collaboration between public and private research

organisations, including SMEs. In addition, as part of a Recovery and Resilience Facility supported reform, Romania adopted Law No. 144/2026 to strengthen links between business and research, requiring at least one third of publicly funded research, development and innovation projects to involve a business enterprise as partner.
